name: Memphite creation theology (Ptah / Shabaka Stone)

earliest_archaeological_evidence.note: British Museum dates the Shabaka Stone itself to 710 BCE, Twenty-fifth Dynasty.

earliest_written_attestation.note: The extant inscription on the Shabaka Stone is the securely dated written attestation used here.

surviving_manuscript_date.note: The surviving witness is an inscribed stone rather than a manuscript; this slot records the physical witness date without implying a papyrus survives.

estimated_composition.method: The British Museum notes that the text in its present form is generally accepted as a composition of Shabaka's own time; whether its religious content embodies older material remains disputed.

tradition_internal_claim.note: The inscription claims Shabaka copied an ancient worm-eaten document. The British Museum treats this antiquarian framing as a known royal-inscription rhetorical device rather than secure evidence of an older physical source.

estimated_oral_origin.method: No oral-origin date is assigned. Possible older Memphite theological content is kept separate from the securely dated inscription.

dating.dating_summary: The surviving Shabaka Stone is securely dated to 710 BCE. Its present literary form is generally treated as Twenty-fifth-Dynasty, while the possible antiquity of some underlying theology remains disputed.

notes: Egyptian creation traditions were plural, not one canonical account. This entity is specifically the Memphite/Ptah tradition preserved on the Shabaka Stone.
